chunks: Applications of LiDAR. The question: What are some applications?
LiDAR gives direct, accurate 3D shape without needing daylight.
So it is used wherever machines must know the shape of the world: cars that detect obstacles, robots that map a warehouse, aircraft that survey terrain, and phones that measure depth for focus.
Each use needs different numbers for range, detail, coverage and speed, so each leads to a different LiDAR design.
Think of reading glasses, binoculars and a wide-angle lens. Reading glasses help up close, binoculars reach far in a narrow view, and a wide lens takes in the whole scene.
LiDARs differ the same way. A phone needs a few meters and tiny size. A highway car needs a long, narrow view. A mapping aircraft needs wide coverage and dense points.
The lens picture does not show that cost and eye safety also limit every design.
The use case drives the specs; the specs drive the architecture (spinning, MEMS, flash, FMCW) and cost.
Reading the diagram left to right is a good template for answering any "design a LiDAR for X" question.
Range: how far away an object can be and still be detected. Reflectivity: the fraction of light an object bounces back.
Black tires return far less than white paint, so range is always quoted for a stated reflectivity. Field of view: how wide and tall an angle the sensor covers.
Point density: how many measured points land on each square meter. Stopping distance: the distance covered during your reaction time plus the distance needed to brake.
How far must a car's LiDAR see? At 100 km/h the car moves 27. 8 m each second. With a 0. 5 seconds reaction time it covers about 13. 9 m before braking starts.
Braking hard on dry road, at 7. 85 m/s², takes another 49 m. The total is about 63 m. At 130 km/h on a wet road it is about 185 m.
That is why highway LiDARs are specified at 150 m or more on a dark, low-reflectivity target. That is the whole idea.

"LiDAR gives direct 3D geometry in any lighting, so it's used wherever machines need to know the shape of the world: autonomous driving and driver assistance, mobile robots and safety scanners, airborne and terrestrial surveying and forestry, drones, and small depth sensors in phones for autofocus and AR.
The use sets the specs: a highway car needs 150 to 250 meters of range, a vacuum robot needs cheap short range 360 degrees, a mapping drone needs point density and accuracy."
